title: Leverage & Perpetuals (Margin & PnL)
objectives: Understand how a perpetual futures contract lets you trade with leverage and no expiry
Calculate PnL, Return on Equity (ROE), and the exact liquidation price of a position
See why leverage multiplies losses just as fast as gains - and how margin calls wipe accounts
Feel the difference between 2x and 20x by watching a position survive or die as price moves

steps.title: Your Pro Sandbox
steps.text: This is your perps desk. You start with $100 of simulated margin and zero real risk.

steps.title: Module Badge
steps.text: LAB P3 badges the leverage lab. Reset brings you back to 10x and a clean position.

steps.title: Leverage & Price Move
steps.text: Pick long or short, then drag leverage and the price move. The liquidation bar shows exactly how close you are to being force-closed.

steps.title: What Just Happened?
steps.text: The explainer calculates whether an ordinary wiggle just liquidated you - and why leverage multiplies the percentage move.

steps.title: Leverage: A Loan That Trades For You
steps.body:
A <Term id="perpetual">perpetual</Term> ('perp') is a contract that lets you bet on a price with no expiry date. You post a small amount of <Term id="margin">margin</Term> (your own money), and the venue lets you control a much larger position through <Term id="leverage">leverage</Term>.

**The core mechanic:**

- You deposit $100 of margin.
- You choose 10x leverage.
- You now control a $1,000 position.
- Every 1% the price moves, your *equity* moves ~10%.

That cuts both ways. A 1% move in your favor = +10% on your money. A 1% move against you = -10% on your money. At 10x, a ~10% adverse move erases your entire margin and you get liquidated.

**Why anyone uses this:** capital efficiency. Instead of tying up $1,000 to trade $1,000, you tie up $100 and keep the other $900 working elsewhere. **Why it destroys people:** the same efficiency means a normal, boring market wiggle becomes a total wipeout. Leverage does not change your win rate - it changes how fast you find out if you were wrong.
hints: Leverage amplifies percentage moves on your EQUITY, not on the position size.
The higher the leverage, the closer your liquidation price sits to entry. 20x can liquidate on a 5% wiggle.

steps.title: PnL, ROE, and the Liquidation Price
steps.body:
Three numbers run every leveraged position:

- **Position size** = margin x leverage. With $100 at 10x, size = $1,000.
- **PnL** = (exit price - entry price) x units held. Long profits when price rises; short profits when it falls.
- **ROE (Return on Equity)** = PnL / margin. This is the number that feels huge at high leverage.

**Liquidation** happens when your losses eat your margin. For a long with maintenance margin, roughly:

`Liquidation Price ≈ Entry x (1 - 1/leverage)`

Run it at different leverage with a $100 margin long entered at $100:

- **2x** → liquidated near $50. Price must halve to kill you.
- **10x** → liquidated near $90. A 10% dip ends you.
- **20x** → liquidated near $95. A 5% dip ends you.

The seductive part: at 20x, a 5% up-move gives you +100% ROE. The lethal part: a 5% down-move gives you -100% and it is over. Same math, opposite mood. Most perp traders do not blow up because they were wrong about direction - they blow up because they were right *eventually* but got <Term id="liquidation">liquidated</Term> before the market agreed.
hints: Memorize the shape: liquidation distance ≈ 1/leverage away from entry.
ROE is PnL over margin. +25% ROE at 5x is just a 5% price move - leverage is doing all the work.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Margin, Maintenance, and the Liquidation Engine
steps.body:
Your collateral is split conceptually into **initial margin** (needed to open) and **maintenance margin** (the floor you must keep). When your equity drops to the maintenance requirement, the liquidation engine fires.

For a long, equity = margin + PnL. As price falls, PnL turns negative and equity shrinks. The instant equity <= maintenance margin, the venue force-closes your position at market - often with a liquidation penalty on top. You do not get liquidated at exactly zero equity; you get liquidated *early*, leaving a buffer to protect the venue from slippage.

**A concrete 10x long, $100 margin, entry $100:**

1. Position size $1,000 (10 SOL-equivalent units).
2. Price drops to $92: PnL = -$80, equity = $20. Danger zone.
3. Price drops to $90: PnL = -$100, equity = $0 - engine liquidates you.

Notice you lost 100% of your money on a mere 10% price drop - a move that a spot holder could shrug off. This is why perps feel like a different sport: the *liquidation engine*, not the market, is your real opponent. Positions are marked against the <Term id="health_factor">health factor</Term> of your margin in real time, and the moment it breaches the floor, discretion disappears and the bot takes over.
hints: You are liquidated at maintenance margin, not at zero. Bankruptcy is early and automatic.
Liquidation penalty fees mean you often lose more than 'all your margin' on paper versus what you deposited.

questions.prompt: You post $100 margin at 10x leverage. What is your position size and what does a 1% favorable price move do to your equity?
questions.explainRight: Correct. Size = margin x leverage = $100 x 10 = $1,000. A 1% price move on a $1,000 position is $10 of PnL, which is +10% on your $100 equity. Leverage scales moves on your margin, not on the position.
questions.explainWrong: Size = margin x leverage = $1,000. A 1% move on $1,000 is $10 PnL, and $10 / $100 equity = +10%. That is the whole point of leverage: it multiplies the percentage move applied to your own capital.

questions.prompt: Using the rule of thumb, roughly where does a 20x LONG entered at $100 get liquidated?
questions.explainRight: Correct. Liquidation distance ≈ 1/leverage = 1/20 = 5%. A long at $100 with 20x leverage is wiped by a move to around $95. At high leverage, terrifyingly small wiggles end positions.
questions.explainWrong: The liquidation distance is roughly 1/leverage from entry. At 20x that is 5%, so a long at $100 dies near $95. Higher leverage means closer liquidation - this is why 20x feels like a coin flip on noise.

questions.prompt: You are 10x long and the price drops 10%. Why are you liquidated even though 10% is a normal market day?
options: Because the exchange decides to liquidate profitable traders
Because a 10% adverse move equals -100% ROE at 10x, wiping your entire margin down to the maintenance floor
Because liquidations only happen on weekends
Because leverage protects you from 10% moves
questions.explainRight: Correct. 10x leverage turns a 10% price move into a 100% move on your equity. Your margin is gone and equity hits the maintenance floor, so the engine liquidates. Leverage does not make you safer - it converts ordinary volatility into account-ending events.
questions.explainWrong: At 10x, a 10% adverse move = -100% ROE. Your equity collapses to the maintenance requirement and the engine force-closes. A 10% day is normal for the market but *fatal* for a 10x position.

questions.prompt: What is the most accurate statement about why leveraged traders blow up?
options: They are always wrong about direction
Leverage does not change your win rate - it changes how much adverse noise you can survive before liquidation, so they die on moves their thesis would eventually have survived
Perps have no liquidation mechanism, so losses are unlimited but reversible
High leverage makes the market move against you more often
questions.explainRight: Correct. Leverage is a survival constraint, not a prediction tool. Many blown accounts were ultimately 'right' - but they were liquidated by normal volatility before the market caught up. Managing liquidation distance matters more than being clever.
questions.explainWrong: Most liquidations are not about being wrong forever - they are about not surviving the journey. Leverage shrinks the noise you can absorb, so ordinary wiggles liquidate positions that a spot holder (or a lower-leverage trader) would have ridden out.
